title: His name is John (Luke 1:57–80)
hook: Zechariah's tongue loosens into a song: the dayspring from on high

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary's song: he has filled the hungry with good things. Your line was the hungry filled. Who did you put good food in front of? Day five hundred seven.

Eight days after the baby is born, the house is full. Neighbors, cousins, the whole extended family, there for the circumcision and the naming. Everybody has an opinion, and everybody agrees: name him Zechariah, after his father. Obviously. Then Elisabeth speaks up: "Not so; but he shall be called John." The relatives push back. Nobody in your family has that name. So they turn to the father, still silent after all these months, and make signs to ask him. And Zechariah, the old priest who couldn't say a word, asks for a writing tablet.
screen: `EIGHT DAYS: A HOUSE FULL OF OPINIONS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "he asked for a writing table, and wrote, saying, His name is John. And they marvelled all." Not his name will be John. His name is John. It's already settled; the angel named him months ago. And in that moment of trust, "his mouth was opened immediately, and his tongue loosed, and he spake, and praised God." Months of silence, and the first thing out of him is praise, and then a song. In Latin it begins Benedictus, blessed, and that's its name. "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel; for he hath visited and redeemed his people." The first half is about all of Israel, God keeping old promises to Abraham and David. Then the old man turns to the child, and the song turns tender: "And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest: for thou shalt go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways." Imagine being eight days old and hearing your job description. And then these lines: "whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us, To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace." Dayspring is an old English word for sunrise, the first light. Christians hear in it Jesus, the light John will point toward. Behind dayspring is the Greek word anatole, a rising. Some readers notice that the old Greek version of the prophets uses the same word for the promised branch from David's line. A sunrise, and a new shoot from an old tree. In Catholic Lauds and in Anglican and Lutheran Morning Prayer, Zechariah's song is still prayed or sung, at the hour when the dayspring actually comes.
screen: then, large: `THE DAYSPRING FROM ON HIGH HATH VISITED US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet the dawn. If it's morning, go to a window or step outside and face the light. If it's not, picture tomorrow's sunrise: the sky going gray, then pale, then gold at the edge. Settle, and breathe. Think of the darkness Zechariah sings about, the shadow some people are sitting in right now. Maybe someone you know. Maybe you. Then let the light come up in your mind, slowly, the way it really does, a little at a time. Light to them that sit in darkness. If you pray, you can greet the morning with Zechariah's words. If you don't, simply watch the light arrive. The bell holds the time.
Benedictus. Latin for blessed, the first word of Zechariah's song when his tongue is loosed, still sung in morning prayer.
Your line: the dayspring from on high. Tomorrow morning, before you check your phone, look at the light for one minute. Let it be the first thing you greet. Day five hundred seven.

howItsDone: The Benedictus is sung or said each morning in several traditions: at Lauds in the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours and at Morning Prayer in Anglican and Lutheran traditions.

original.note: Greek: a rising, sunrise, the east. the dayspring of Zechariah's song.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old word nobody uses, dayspring.
what it means: Zechariah's song pictures God's mercy rising like the sun on people sitting in darkness, and his son going ahead to prepare the way.
what a scholar hears: anatole means a rising, and the old Greek version of the prophets also used it for the promised branch from David's line.

notes: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew tsemach ('Branch') as anatole in Jeremiah 23:5 and Zechariah 3:8, 6:12. Confirm.
'Nine months of silence' is approximate (from the temple scene through John's eighth day).
Daily use of the Benedictus at Lauds/Morning Prayer. Confirm for Lutheran practice.
The circumcision on the eighth day (1:59) is mentioned as the occasion; described neutrally.
